positions/pelagianism/oneLine: Human nature, created good by God, retains the ability to obey God’s commands; grace is God’s gift of nature, law, Christ’s teaching and example, and forgiveness.
positions/pelagianism/coreClaims/0: Adam’s sin harmed his descendants by bad example, not by inherited guilt or a corrupted nature.
positions/pelagianism/coreClaims/1: God, being just, commands nothing impossible; therefore human beings can avoid sin if they will.
positions/pelagianism/coreClaims/2: Grace includes free will itself, the law, the teaching and example of Christ, and the forgiveness of past sins in baptism.
positions/pelagianism/coreClaims/3: Christians are called to a demanding, perfectionist holiness without excuse.
positions/pelagianism/origin: Taught in Rome c.380-410 by the British ascetic Pelagius and his associate Caelestius, in reaction to moral laxity and to fatalistic readings of Augustine’s "give what you command"; developed polemically by Julian of Eclanum.
positions/pelagianism/strongestArguments: It takes divine commands seriously: "ought" implies "can", and a just God does not punish people for what they could not avoid.
It protects God’s justice from the charge of condemning infants and others for a sin they did not personally commit.
It produces moral seriousness and resists using human weakness as an excuse for sin.
positions/pelagianism/strongestObjection: Augustine: it makes Christ’s grace unnecessary and Christ merely a teacher and example (Gal 2:21).
It cannot explain the universality of sin or the Church’s practice of baptising infants "for the remission of sins".
Paul describes a will unable to do the good it desires (Rom 7:14-25) and salvation as wholly of grace (Eph 2:8-9).
positions/pelagianism/responses/0: Pelagians replied that grace is indeed needed and everywhere present — in nature, law and Christ — and that Augustine’s view slides into Manichaean fatalism.
positions/pelagianism/responses/1: Some modern historians argue Pelagius has been caricatured and that his surviving letters are more grace-conscious than his opponents allowed.
positions/pelagianism/consequences/0: Condemned at Carthage (418), by Pope Zosimus (418) and at Ephesus (431); "Pelagian" became a byword for moralism in Western theology.
positions/pelagianism/consequences/1: The controversy pushed Augustine into his strongest statements on original sin and predestination, shaping the entire Western debate.
positions/augustinianism/oneLine: Since Adam’s fall all humanity is bound in sin; only God’s unmerited, inwardly efficacious grace heals and frees the will, and God freely predestines those he saves.
positions/augustinianism/coreClaims/0: All humanity sinned "in Adam" and inherits a wounded nature and guilt (original sin).
positions/augustinianism/coreClaims/1: The fallen will is free to sin but not able to love God without grace that "goes before" (prevenient) and accompanies it.
positions/augustinianism/coreClaims/2: Grace is not merely external teaching but an inner delight and charity "poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit" (Rom 5:5).
positions/augustinianism/coreClaims/3: God, from eternity and without regard to merit, predestines some to salvation and grants them perseverance; others are justly left in the mass of perdition.
positions/augustinianism/origin: Developed by Augustine of Hippo from To Simplician (396) through the anti-Pelagian writings (412-430), out of his reading of Paul and his own conversion.
positions/augustinianism/strongestArgume: It does justice to Paul’s account of sin and grace and to the Church’s prayers: we pray for conversion because God gives it.
It safeguards grace as wholly unmerited — "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Cor 4:7).
It matches the experience of conversion as rescue rather than achievement, and grounds humility and assurance in God.
positions/augustinianism/strongestObject: Eastern fathers never shared Augustine’s account of inherited guilt or his strong predestinarianism; many Orthodox see it as a Western distortion.
Pelagians and later Arminians object that it makes God responsible for the damnation of those he passes over.
Critics argue it depends on a mistranslation of Romans 5:12 ("in whom all sinned") in the Latin.
positions/augustinianism/responses/0: Augustinians reply that condemnation is just because all are guilty; God’s mercy to some wrongs no one (Matt 20:15).
positions/augustinianism/responses/1: They argue that the doctrine of original sin does not rest on one Latin phrase but on the whole Adam-Christ parallel and the universality of death and sin.
positions/augustinianism/consequences/0: Became the framework of Latin theology; approved in moderated form at Orange (529).
positions/augustinianism/consequences/1: Claimed by Gottschalk, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin and Jansen alike, each in different ways — the common root of later Western divisions.
positions/semi-pelagianism/oneLine: Grace is necessary for salvation, but the first movement of faith (initium fidei) can arise from the human will, which God then assists; predestination follows foreseen response.
positions/semi-pelagianism/coreClaims/0: Grace is indispensable for completing salvation.
positions/semi-pelagianism/coreClaims/1: The beginning of faith or of the good will can come from the free will, sometimes before grace, sometimes after.
positions/semi-pelagianism/coreClaims/2: God wills all to be saved; predestination is based on foreknowledge of human response.
positions/semi-pelagianism/coreClaims/3: Perseverance is not an irresistible gift to a fixed number.
positions/semi-pelagianism/origin: A 17th-century label (from the Molinist controversy) for the view of monks around Marseille and Lérins — John Cassian (Conference 13, c.427), Vincent of Lérins, later Faustus of Riez (On Grace, c.474) — who resisted Augustine’s late predestinarian writings.
positions/semi-pelagianism/strongestArgu: It honours Scripture’s calls to "turn" and "seek" and God’s universal saving will.
It reflects monastic experience of real cooperation in the spiritual struggle.
It avoids making God the cause of reprobation.
positions/semi-pelagianism/strongestObje: Prosper of Aquitaine and the Council of Orange: it makes the decisive beginning of salvation a human work, so grace responds to merit.
Augustinians: it contradicts "No one can come to me unless the Father draws him" (John 6:44).
Reformation theologians later charged late-medieval and Catholic theology with semi-Pelagianism (Catholics deny the charge).
positions/semi-pelagianism/responses/0: Defenders point out that the label is anachronistic and that Cassian is venerated as a saint in East and West.
positions/semi-pelagianism/responses/1: Many Orthodox note that Cassian’s synergy is closer to the Eastern consensus than either Pelagius or Augustine.
positions/semi-pelagianism/consequences/: "Semi-Pelagian" became a polemical charge in the Gottschalk, Reformation, Molinist and Calvinist-Arminian disputes.
positions/orange-semi-augustinianism/one: Even the beginning of faith is a gift of prevenient grace, and all the baptised, aided by Christ, can and should fulfil what pertains to salvation; no one is predestined to evil.
positions/orange-semi-augustinianism/cor: Through Adam’s sin free will was weakened so that no one can believe or love God without prevenient grace.
The beginning of faith and the desire for baptism are gifts of grace, not natural achievements.
After baptism, by Christ’s grace, all can and ought to fulfil what pertains to salvation if they will labour faithfully.
Predestination of anyone to evil by divine power is anathematised.
positions/orange-semi-augustinianism/ori: Canons drafted by Caesarius of Arles from Augustine and Prosper of Aquitaine, adopted at Orange on 3 July 529 and confirmed by Pope Boniface II in 531.
positions/orange-semi-augustinianism/str: It preserves the priority of grace while avoiding double predestination.
It joins grace with sacramental and ethical responsibility in the life of the baptised.
Its papal confirmation gave it lasting authority in Catholic theology.
Strict Augustinians (Gottschalk, some Reformed) see it as softening Augustine on irresistible grace and particular predestination.
Arminians and Orthodox ask whether it leaves room for genuine human response.
Its canons were forgotten for centuries, raising questions about its real influence on medieval theology.
positions/orange-semi-augustinianism/res: Catholic theologians answer that Orange defines the necessary minimum, leaving freedom for Thomist, Molinist and other schools.
Reformers like Calvin cited Orange approvingly as evidence that sola gratia was ancient catholic teaching.
positions/orange-semi-augustinianism/con: Ended the semi-Pelagian controversy in Gaul.
Rediscovered in the 16th century and invoked by both Trent and the Reformers.
positions/gottschalk-double-predestinati: Gottschalk’s twofold predestination
gemina praedestinatio
double predestination
God has eternally predestined the elect to life and the reprobate to death; Christ died only for the elect, and God’s will to save is not universal.
Predestination is "twofold" (gemina): of the elect to glory and of the reprobate to just punishment.
God’s immutable will cannot be frustrated; therefore he does not will the salvation of those who perish.
Christ’s blood was shed for the elect alone.
Gottschalk claimed to be simply repeating Augustine and Fulgentius.
Romans 9:13-23
Proverbs 16:4
Ephesians 1:4-11
Taught by Gottschalk of Orbais (c.808-c.867), a Saxon monk, from the 840s; condemned at Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849) under Archbishop Hincmar of Reims, and imprisoned for life.
Ratramnus of Corbie (in part)
Prudentius of Troyes
Remigius of Lyon
Lupus of Ferrières
It applies Augustine’s logic consistently: if God’s will is omnipotent, those he wills to save are saved.
It finds support in Augustine and Fulgentius and in Pauline texts.
It protects God’s sovereignty and the effectiveness of Christ’s death.
Hincmar and John Scotus Eriugena: it makes God the author of damnation and contradicts 1 Timothy 2:4.
It removes the motive for moral effort and pastoral care.
Orange (529) had condemned predestination to evil.
Gottschalk distinguished predestination to just punishment (for sin) from predestination to sin, which he denied.
The councils of Valence (855) and Langres (859) defended a qualified double predestination, showing the Carolingian church was divided.
First great medieval predestination controversy; led to a compromise at Tuzey (860).
Reformed theologians later rehabilitated Gottschalk as a forerunner.
positions/thomist-grace/oneLine: Grace perfects nature: God’s gratuitous grace moves the free will from within, so that faith, charity and merit are wholly God’s gift and genuinely the believer’s act.
positions/thomist-grace/coreClaims/0: Human beings need grace both to heal fallen nature and to be elevated to a supernatural end (the beatific vision).
positions/thomist-grace/coreClaims/1: Actual grace moves the will and habitual (sanctifying) grace transforms the soul; justification includes forgiveness and infused charity.
positions/thomist-grace/coreClaims/2: Merit is real but founded entirely on grace: God crowns his own gifts.
positions/thomist-grace/coreClaims/3: Predestination is God’s gratuitous plan to bring some to glory; later Dominicans (Báñez) speak of "physical premotion".
positions/thomist-grace/origin: Thomas Aquinas’ Summa Theologiae (I q. 23; I-II qq. 109-114, c.1265-1274), systematised by Domingo Báñez (1528-1604) and the Dominican school.
positions/thomist-grace/strongestArgumen: It integrates Augustine’s priority of grace with a robust account of human nature and cooperation.
Its primary/secondary causation model explains how God and the creature can both be fully the cause of a good act.
It underlies much of Trent’s decree on justification.
positions/thomist-grace/strongestObjecti: Molinists: physical premotion seems to make human freedom illusory and God the cause of sin by withholding grace.
Protestants: infused grace and merit confuse justification with sanctification.
Orthodox: its created-grace framework obscures participation in God’s uncreated energies.
positions/thomist-grace/responses/0: Thomists answer that God’s causality does not compete with creaturely freedom but grounds it.
positions/thomist-grace/responses/1: Catholic theologians note that Trent explicitly says eternal life is both grace and reward.
positions/thomist-grace/consequences/1: One pole of the De Auxiliis controversy (1597-1607).
